title: Gastrointestinal Organs and Glands
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the gross anatomy of the stomach and duodenum, the peritoneal relationships of the abdominal gut, the liver and biliary tree, the features that set the colon apart from the small intestine, and the three major salivary glands. Board questions rarely ask for a structure in isolation. They give a finding, such as bilious or nonbilious vomiting, jaundice with or without pancreatitis, flank bruising, right lower quadrant pain, or facial weakness with a parotid mass, and expect you to place the lesion. If you know where each organ sits, what lies next to it, and whether peritoneum covers it, you can explain those findings by location.

Branches of the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery (GI-5)
Cranial nerves VII and IX and the parasympathetic ganglia of the head

connections.to: The gut in the body cavities (GI-4)
connections.how: The peritoneal sacs, omenta, and ligaments described there are the same folds that make organs in this chapter intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal.
The major duodenal papilla marks the change from celiac to superior mesenteric supply, and the gastroduodenal artery behind the duodenal bulb explains bleeding from posterior ulcers.
The level at which a stone lodges in the biliary tree decides whether the patient has colic, cholecystitis, jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.
Duct anatomy and the tight parotid capsule explain the pain of parotitis and why stones favor the submandibular gland.
The bile duct runs in or behind the pancreatic head, so a mass there causes obstructive jaundice.

terms.def: An organ almost completely covered by visceral peritoneum and suspended by a mesentery or ligament, which leaves it mobile.
An organ that once had a mesentery but was pressed against the posterior body wall during development, so that its peritoneum fused with the parietal peritoneum and it became fixed.
The dilated, mobile first 2 cm or so of the superior part of the duodenum, just beyond the pylorus.
The elevation on the posteromedial wall of the descending duodenum where the hepatopancreatic ampulla opens.
The short dilated channel formed where the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct unite before opening into the duodenum.
The smooth muscle sphincter around the terminal bile duct, the terminal pancreatic duct, and the ampulla that controls flow into the duodenum.
The transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver where the portal vein and hepatic artery enter and the hepatic ducts and lymphatics leave.
The part of the diaphragmatic surface of the liver that lies directly against the diaphragm without a peritoneal covering, bounded by the layers of the coronary ligament.
Three flat bands into which the outer longitudinal muscle of the cecum and colon is gathered.
The sacculations of the colonic wall produced because the taeniae are shorter than the bowel they run along.
The surface point one third of the way along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marking the usual position of the base of the appendix.
The duct of the parotid gland (Stensen duct), which crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.

sections.title: Parts of the stomach and the four parts of the duodenum

blocks.text: The stomach is the dilated part of the foregut between the esophagus and the duodenum. Its regions are defined by position. The cardia surrounds the cardial orifice where the esophagus enters. The fundus is the dome that rises above the level of that orifice under the left hemidiaphragm, which is why swallowed air collects there in an upright patient. The body is the large central part, and the pyloric part follows it: the wide pyloric antrum, the narrower pyloric canal, and the pylorus, a thickened ring of circular smooth muscle that meters chyme into the duodenum. The short lesser curvature faces right and the long greater curvature faces left; the angular incisure, a notch on the lesser curvature, marks where body becomes antrum.

The regions differ in function as well as shape. Parietal cells, which secrete acid and intrinsic factor, and chief cells, which secrete pepsinogen, are concentrated in the fundus and body. Gastrin-secreting G cells lie in the antrum. This is why resection or atrophy of the body and fundus impairs acid and intrinsic factor secretion, while antral disease affects gastrin.

The duodenum is about 25 cm long and curves in a C around the head of the pancreas. Its parts are best learned by what each one touches, because questions turn on those relationships. The major duodenal papilla lies on the posteromedial wall of the descending (second) part. Just distal to it, the duodenum changes from foregut to midgut, and its arterial supply changes from celiac branches (superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries) to superior mesenteric branches (inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries). A minor papilla about 2 cm above the major one drains the accessory pancreatic duct.

blocks.text: Location also explains the color of vomitus. Bile enters at the second part, so an obstruction proximal to the papilla, such as infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, produces nonbilious vomiting, while most duodenal atresias lie distal to the papilla and produce bilious vomiting. Ulcers favor the bulb because it receives acidic chyme from the pylorus before pancreatic bicarbonate arrives at the papilla. An anterior bulb ulcer tends to perforate into the peritoneal cavity, whereas a posterior ulcer tends to bleed from the gastroduodenal artery.

blocks.predict: An infant vomits forcefully after every feed, and the vomitus contains no bile. Where along the stomach and duodenum must the obstruction lie?
blocks.explain: Proximal to the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, because bile only enters the lumen there; the pylorus is the classic site.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on bilious and nonbilious vomiting and the duodenum table.

blocks.text: The peritoneum is a serous membrane: parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall, and visceral peritoneum covers organs. An intraperitoneal organ is almost completely wrapped in visceral peritoneum and hangs from a mesentery or peritoneal ligament, so it moves with posture and peristalsis. A retroperitoneal organ lies behind the parietal peritoneum, covered by it only on its anterior surface, and is fixed to the posterior body wall.

Retroperitoneal organs come in two kinds. Primarily retroperitoneal organs, such as the kidneys, ureters, suprarenal glands, aorta, and inferior vena cava, developed behind the peritoneum and never had a mesentery. Secondarily retroperitoneal organs began on a mesentery and were later pressed against the posterior wall as the gut rotated and grew. Their mesentery fused with the parietal peritoneum to form a fusion fascia.

blocks.text: The distinction has clinical consequences because the retroperitoneum is outside the peritoneal cavity. Blood or enzyme-rich fluid from a retroperitoneal organ tracks through retroperitoneal fat instead of spreading over the peritoneal surfaces, so peritoneal signs may be slight or delayed. Hemorrhagic pancreatitis can track to the flanks and produce flank bruising (Grey Turner sign). A perforation of a retroperitoneal duodenal segment, or a crush injury of the duodenum against the vertebral column in blunt trauma, can leak into the retroperitoneum without free air under the diaphragm, while an anterior perforation of the intraperitoneal bulb releases air into the peritoneal cavity. Mobility follows the same rule: intraperitoneal segments on long mesenteries, such as the sigmoid colon, can twist (volvulus), whereas fixed retroperitoneal segments cannot.

blocks.title: Worked example: where did the air go?
blocks.text: Two patients have perforated duodenal ulcers. In the first, an upright chest film shows air under the right hemidiaphragm and the abdomen is rigid. In the second, there is no free air, but CT shows gas around the right kidney. Step 1: free subdiaphragmatic air means the leak entered the peritoneal cavity, so the ulcer was on the anterior wall of the intraperitoneal duodenal bulb. Step 2: gas around the kidney means the leak entered the retroperitoneum, so the perforation was in a retroperitoneal segment, the fixed distal first part or the second part. Step 3: the second patient has fewer peritoneal signs because the retroperitoneum lacks the parietal peritoneal surface that, when irritated, produces guarding and rigidity.

sections.title: The liver and the path of bile to the duodenum

blocks.text: The liver, the largest gland in the body (about 1.5 kg), has four anatomic lobes. The falciform ligament divides the right lobe from the left lobe on the diaphragmatic surface. On the visceral surface, the caudate lobe lies above the porta hepatis between the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum, and the quadrate lobe lies below the porta between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres. Surgeons use a functional division instead: a plane from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava (Cantlie line) separates functional right and left livers, each with its own portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct branches. The quadrate lobe then belongs to the left liver, and the caudate lobe drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

The liver develops within the ventral mesentery, so its peritoneal folds (falciform, coronary, and triangular ligaments and the lesser omentum) are remnants of that mesentery. The two layers of the coronary ligament separate widely on the posterosuperior surface and leave the bare area, where liver tissue touches the diaphragm directly. The porta hepatis is the hilum of the liver. The portal vein and proper hepatic artery enter there and the right and left hepatic ducts leave, all carried in the free edge of the lesser omentum, the hepatoduodenal ligament. In that ligament the bile duct lies anterior and to the right, the hepatic artery anterior and to the left, and the portal vein posterior. The hepatic veins do not use the porta; they leave the posterior surface directly into the inferior vena cava.

blocks.caption: Between meals the sphincter is closed, so bile backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder for storage and concentration.

blocks.text: The sphincter of Oddi includes separate muscle around the end of the bile duct, the end of the pancreatic duct, and the ampulla. Cholecystokinin (CCK), released by the duodenum when fat and protein arrive, contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter, so bile reaches the lumen when it is needed for fat digestion.

Because all bile funnels into one duct that shares an outlet with the pancreas, the level of an obstruction predicts its effects (table). A common bile duct block raises conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), darkens the urine (conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and filtered), and makes stools pale because no bilirubin reaches the gut to form stercobilin. A tumor of the pancreatic head compresses the bile duct slowly, so the gallbladder distends without inflammation and may be palpable and painless (Courvoisier sign).

blocks.predict: A stone lodges in the cystic duct. Why does the patient have pain but no jaundice?
blocks.explain: Bile from the liver still flows down the common hepatic and common bile ducts to the duodenum; only the gallbladder is cut off, and it contracts painfully against the stone.

sections.title: Features of the colon and the position of the appendix

blocks.text: Both the small and large intestine have an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle, but in the cecum and colon the longitudinal layer is gathered into three flat bands about 1 cm wide, the taeniae coli (named taenia mesocolica, taenia omentalis, and taenia libera). Because the taeniae are shorter than the wall they run along, they pull it into a series of pouches, the haustra. Small fat-filled tags of peritoneum, the omental appendices (appendices epiploicae), hang from the colonic surface. None of these three features is found on the jejunum or ileum, so any one of them identifies colon at surgery or in a specimen.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the colon from the small intestine
rows: No plicae circulares or villi; straight crypts rich in goblet cells
Plicae cross the full width of the lumen
Haustral folds cross only part of the lumen

blocks.caption: Taeniae, haustra, and omental appendices are the gross features; the rest support the distinction.

blocks.text: The taeniae begin at the base of the appendix and run along the colon to the rectosigmoid junction, where they spread out into a continuous longitudinal layer again. This is why the rectum and the appendix lack taeniae and haustra. The wall between the taeniae has a thinner muscle coat, and where the vasa recta penetrate it the wall is weakest, so colonic diverticula (herniations of mucosa and submucosa without muscle) form at these points, most often in the sigmoid colon.

The vermiform appendix is a narrow blind tube, about 6 to 10 cm long, arising from the posteromedial wall of the cecum below the ileocecal junction. Its tip is variable: most often retrocecal, but it may lie in the pelvis, below the cecum, or beside the terminal ileum. Its base, however, is constant, because all three taeniae converge on it, and a surgeon who follows the taeniae down the cecum will reach it. The surface marking of the base is McBurney point, one third of the way along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is supplied by the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery running in the mesoappendix. It is an end artery, so when obstruction and swelling compress it the wall becomes ischemic and can necrose and perforate.

blocks.text: The variable tip changes the findings. A retrocecal appendix lies on the iliopsoas, so extending the right hip stretches the inflamed tissue and causes pain (psoas sign), while anterior tenderness may be mild. A pelvic appendix can lie on the obturator internus, so internal rotation of the flexed right hip causes pain (obturator sign), and tenderness may be felt mainly on rectal examination.

sections.title: The major salivary glands, their ducts, and the facial nerve in the parotid

blocks.text: Three paired major glands produce most of the roughly 1 to 1.5 L of saliva secreted daily; minor glands in the lips, cheeks, and palate add the rest. The glands differ in cell type: serous acini secrete a watery fluid rich in salivary amylase, and mucous acini secrete viscous mucins. The parotid is purely serous, the submandibular gland is mixed but mostly serous, and the sublingual gland is mixed but mostly mucous.

blocks.text: The parotid duct crosses the masseter about a fingerbreadth below the zygomatic arch, then pierces the buccinator; pus appears at its opening in bacterial parotitis. The submandibular duct is long and runs upward from the gland to the floor of the mouth, and its saliva is more viscous and more alkaline, with more calcium; these features slow flow and favor precipitation, which is why about 80 to 90% of salivary stones form in this gland. The lingual nerve loops under the submandibular duct, so it is at risk when the duct is opened.

The facial nerve (CN VII) leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, enters the posterior surface of the parotid, and divides inside the gland into a plexus that gives five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. These branches emerge from the anterior border of the gland and fan out to the muscles of facial expression. The nerve only passes through; it does not supply the parotid, whose secretomotor fibers come from CN IX. From superficial to deep, the facial nerve plexus, the retromandibular vein, and the external carotid artery all lie within the gland.

blocks.caption: Submandibular and sublingual glands use CN VII: chorda tympani, lingual nerve, submandibular ganglion.

blocks.text: Because the nerve runs through the gland, parotid disease can reach it. Most salivary tumors arise in the parotid, and most are benign; the commonest, pleomorphic adenoma, pushes nerve branches aside. A malignant tumor such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma can infiltrate the nerve, so facial weakness with a parotid mass suggests malignancy. Damage within the gland, from tumor or surgery, gives a lower motor neuron palsy that includes the forehead. A late complication of parotidectomy is gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome): cut parasympathetic fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve regrow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin, so eating causes local sweating and flushing. The gland is also enclosed in a tight fascial sheath from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, so inflammation such as mumps raises pressure and causes pain that worsens with chewing.

blocks.predict: A patient with a firm parotid mass cannot wrinkle the forehead, close the eye tightly, or raise the mouth corner on that side. Upper or lower motor neuron pattern, and why is the mass concerning?
blocks.explain: Lower motor neuron: the nerve is damaged in the gland, distal to the brainstem, so every branch including the temporal is affected. Benign tumors usually displace the nerve, so paralysis suggests an invading malignancy.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on parotid tumors.

integration.text: Embryology explains most of this chapter's anatomy. The stomach and the liver develop in the dorsal and ventral mesenteries, and gut rotation presses the duodenum, pancreas, and ascending and descending colon against the posterior wall, where their mesenteries fuse. That single event decides which organs are mobile, which bleed into the retroperitoneum, and which can twist. The major papilla sits at the foregut to midgut junction, so it also marks the change in arterial supply (celiac to superior mesenteric) and the boundary between nonbilious and bilious vomiting. The taeniae and haustra reflect how the colonic muscle is arranged, and the points where vessels pierce that muscle are where diverticula form.

Pathology and physiology then work through location. A gallstone causes colic, jaundice, or pancreatitis according to the duct it blocks, and the effects follow bile and bilirubin physiology: conjugated bilirubin in the urine, no stercobilin in the stool. Pain from the appendix or gallbladder changes character when inflammation reaches somatically innervated parietal peritoneum. In the head, the facial nerve's course through the parotid and the separate CN IX and CN VII secretomotor pathways explain why a parotid tumor can cause facial palsy even though the facial nerve does not supply the gland, and why mumps causes a painful, tense gland.

summary: The stomach has cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part (antrum, canal, pylorus); acid and intrinsic factor come from the fundus and body, gastrin from the antrum.

The duodenum has four parts: the ulcer-prone bulb, the descending part with the major papilla, the horizontal part between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, and the ascending part ending at the suspensory ligament.
Obstruction proximal to the major papilla gives nonbilious vomiting; obstruction distal to it gives bilious vomiting.

Secondarily retroperitoneal organs (duodenum parts 2 to 4, pancreas except the tail, ascending and descending colon) lost their mesenteries by fusion; the rectum is covered progressively less toward its lower third.
Retroperitoneal bleeding or perforation tracks behind the peritoneum, giving flank signs and fewer peritoneal signs, without free air under the diaphragm.

The liver has right, left, caudate, and quadrate anatomic lobes; the porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic ducts, while the hepatic veins drain directly to the inferior vena cava.
Bile flows from the hepatic ducts to the common hepatic duct, joins the cystic duct as the common bile duct, and meets the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater under the sphincter of Oddi.
Taeniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices identify the colon; the taeniae converge at the constant base of the appendix, marked at McBurney point.
The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar; the submandibular duct opens beside the lingual frenulum and is the usual site of stones.
The facial nerve divides into its five branches inside the parotid without supplying it, so parotid malignancy or surgery can cause lower motor neuron facial palsy.

verify: Lengths and vertebral levels of the duodenal parts follow Moore and are approximate; other sources give slightly different figures.
Liver mass (about 1.5 kg) and appendix length (about 6 to 10 cm) vary among references.
The percentage of appendices that are retrocecal (often quoted near 65%) varies widely between anatomical series, so the chapter states only that retrocecal is most common.
The share of salivary stones in the submandibular gland is quoted from about 80% to 92%; the chapter uses about 80 to 90%.
Daily saliva volume is quoted from about 0.8 to 1.5 L; the chapter uses roughly 1 to 1.5 L.
